[PATH:empirical] American Community Survey (ACS) microdata combined with zip-code-level business pattern data from the Census Bureau (e.g., County Business Patterns) to estimate local employment and wage changes in low-skilled services (e.g., food preparation, personal services) at the census tract or zip code level, differentiating between high-skilled immigrant clusters and non-cluster areas within the same metro region. — This would allow direct empirical testing of whether the demand effect is localized to residential clusters of high-skilled immigrants, rather than diffusing across the entire metro area. By comparing tracts with high versus low shares of high-skilled immigrants over time (2010-2023), one can isolate the spatial specificity of the hypothesized effect.

[PATH:empirical] A difference-in-differences or event-study analysis using the H-1B visa lottery as a natural experiment, linking lottery outcomes to subsequent changes in low-skilled service employment and wages at the neighborhood level (e.g., using data from the Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics (LEHD) program or Quarterly Workforce Indicators). — This approach would exploit exogenous variation in high-skilled immigration to identify causal effects on local low-skilled service demand. Analyzing outcomes by neighborhood (e.g., within 1-2 km of high-skilled immigrant residences) versus metro-wide would directly test the spatial concentration claim.

[PATH:literature] Ethnographic or survey-based studies of local service providers (e.g., restaurants, cleaning services, ride-hail drivers) in neighborhoods with high concentrations of high-skilled immigrants versus comparable neighborhoods without such clusters, to capture qualitative evidence of changes in demand and business strategies. — Existing case-study literature (e.g., on gentrification and immigrant enclaves) may provide complementary qualitative evidence on whether demand effects are hyper-localized. Synthesizing findings from studies in the specified cities (SF Bay Area, Seattle, NYC, Boston) could corroborate or challenge the hypothesis, especially if those studies document spatial spillovers or lack thereof.
